title: Networking (DNS, TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS, TLS, WebSockets, long-polling/SSE)
relevance: High — assumed in nearly every HLD round; real-time protocol choice is probed in chat, notifications, feeds, and collaborative apps (campus + experienced, FAANG and Indian product cos).
company_notes: Campus/new-grad HLD: usually unspoken background; explicit “type a URL” or TCP vs UDP still appears at some Indian product cos and mid-tier FAANG-adjacent rounds. Experienced/mid-level HLD: protocol choice is a standard deep dive in chat, notifications, live feeds, multiplayer, and collaborative docs; HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 and WebSocket scaling separate strong answers. Foundational in every design round; real-time protocol tradeoffs appear when the prompt mentions live, push, or instant.

phases.goal: Establish DNS, TCP vs UDP, HTTPS/TLS basics, and the end-to-end browser request path.

must_hit.point: DNS maps names to IPs via recursive resolvers over a hierarchy (root → TLD → authoritative); TTL caching speeds lookups but delays IP/record change propagation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks root → TLD → authoritative and names TTL as both a cache win and a propagation delay.

must_hit.point: TCP is connection-oriented, ordered, and reliable (3-way handshake, ACKs, retransmission, congestion control) and is the default for HTTP, DBs, and most APIs; UDP is connectionless, best-effort, low overhead (DNS queries, VoIP, gaming, QUIC under HTTP/3).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts reliability vs low overhead and gives fitting use cases for each transport.

must_hit.point: A browser request path is DNS → TCP (and TLS if HTTPS) → HTTP request/response; keep-alive and multiplexing amortize handshake cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders the stages correctly and notes handshake amortization via keep-alive or multiplexing.

must_hit.point: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: the cert validates identity; asymmetric crypto negotiates a session key, then symmetric encryption carries bulk data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates identity (cert), key negotiation (asymmetric), and bulk encryption (symmetric).

probes: What happens when you type https://example.com into a browser?
When would you choose TCP vs UDP in a system design?

hints.1: Start from name resolution, then connection setup, then the application request.
hints.2: Sequence: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS if HTTPS → HTTP GET/response; for transport, ask whether you need ordered reliable delivery or can tolerate loss.
hints.3: DNS (root→TLD→authoritative, TTL cache) → TCP 3-way handshake → TLS (cert + session key) → HTTP; TCP for correctness-sensitive paths, UDP for DNS/VoIP/gaming/QUIC.

phases.goal: Explain how HTTP versions, TLS RTTs, and real-time push mechanisms actually work.

must_hit.point: HTTP/1.1 needs many connections because of head-of-line blocking; HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one TCP connection but still suffers TCP HOL; HTTP/3/QUIC runs over UDP so one lost packet does not stall all streams.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names HOL at HTTP/1.1, residual TCP HOL under HTTP/2, and stream-level loss isolation under HTTP/3/QUIC.

must_hit.point: TLS adds RTTs (TLS 1.3 is about 1-RTT; session resumption and 0-RTT help); keep-alive, session tickets, and HTTP/2+ connection reuse mitigate handshake cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions TLS 1.3 ≈ 1-RTT and at least one mitigation (resumption, 0-RTT, keep-alive, or connection reuse).

must_hit.point: HTTP is request/response and client-initiated—the server cannot freely push without a held or upgraded connection.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States that plain HTTP cannot server-push without long-held or upgraded connections.

must_hit.point: Short polling asks on an interval; long polling holds until data or timeout; SSE is long-lived HTTP server→client with EventSource auto-reconnect; WebSockets upgrade HTTP to a full-duplex persistent channel.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines each of the four patterns with directionality and connection lifetime.

probes: Why does HTTP/3 exist if HTTP/2 already multiplexes streams?
How do short polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSockets differ mechanistically?

hints.1: Think about where blocking happens—application layer vs transport layer—and who can send without a new request.
hints.2: HTTP/2 multiplexes on TCP so a lost packet still stalls the connection; map each real-time option to interval poll, held request, one-way stream, or upgraded duplex.
hints.3: HTTP/3/QUIC over UDP isolates loss per stream; short poll = interval, long poll = hold until event, SSE = server→client EventSource, WebSocket = HTTP upgrade to full-duplex.

phases.goal: Choose transports and real-time protocols with explicit costs, and apply REST vs RPC and DNS TTL tradeoffs.

must_hit.point: Default to HTTP with SSE or long-poll unless you truly need bidirectional low-latency streams; WebSockets add fan-out, reconnect, and sticky-routing cost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers HTTP-family push for one-way updates and reserves WebSockets for true bidirectional need, naming scaling costs.

must_hit.point: High DNS TTL means stale IPs after failover/deploy; low TTL means more resolver load and slightly higher p99 latency.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both sides of the TTL knob: freshness/failover vs resolver load and latency.

must_hit.point: REST/HTTP wins public APIs and tooling; RPC (e.g. gRPC) is common inside the datacenter; remote calls are not local calls because of network failure, latency, and partial failure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Puts REST at the public boundary and RPC inside, and rejects “remote = local”.

must_hit.point: Domain sharding helped HTTP/1.1 connection limits but can hurt HTTP/2, which wants fewer connections to multiplex efficiently.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains sharding as an HTTP/1.1 workaround that fights HTTP/2’s single-connection multiplexing model.

probes: Why not always use WebSockets for real-time features?
For a public API vs internal service calls, when do you pick REST vs RPC?

hints.1: Ask whether both sides must push often, and what breaks when connections and DNS records change.
hints.2: Compare server→client-only needs (SSE/long-poll) vs duplex (WebSocket); separate public HTTP tooling from internal RPC and TTL freshness vs load.
hints.3: Avoid always-on WebSockets due to state, reconnect storms, sticky LB affinity, and scaling pain; REST publicly, RPC internally; high TTL stalls failover, low TTL loads resolvers.

phases.goal: Apply protocol choice to concrete product scenarios and load-balancer implications.

must_hit.point: For real-time scenarios (e.g. stock ticker, WhatsApp-style chat, unread badge, QR login wait), pick short poll, long poll, SSE, or WebSocket and state one scaling downside of the pick.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Assigns a fitting protocol per scenario and names a concrete downside (empty polls, held connections, one-way limit, or sticky/fan-out cost).

must_hit.point: Contrast L4 vs L7 load balancing for WebSocket vs plain REST; sticky sessions may be needed for connection state and that hurts failure domains.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties WebSocket affinity/state to L7/sticky needs and notes the failure-domain cost.

must_hit.point: HTTPS is non-negotiable for auth cookies and PII; a cert proves server identity; handshake cost is mitigated with keep-alive, session tickets, and HTTP/2+/connection reuse.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links HTTPS to cookie/PII safety, cert identity, and at least one handshake mitigation.

must_hit.point: Scaling many open sockets needs connection servers, pub/sub fan-out, heartbeats, timeouts, and regional gateways—estimate RAM/FD cost per connection.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists connection-server/fan-out/heartbeat patterns rather than “just open sockets on every app box.”

probes: For a stock ticker vs WhatsApp-style chat vs an unread badge, which real-time protocol do you choose and why?
How would you load-balance WebSockets differently from plain REST, and when do sticky sessions hurt?

hints.1: Classify each feature as client-pull, server→client push, or frequent bidirectional push.
hints.2: Unread badge/ticker often SSE or long-poll; chat needs WebSockets; then ask whether the LB must be L7-aware and sticky.
hints.3: Ticker/notifications → SSE (or long-poll fallback); chat/collab → WebSocket with sticky/fan-out cost; REST can be L4/L7 without affinity, WebSockets often need sticky L7 and that couples failure domains.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: TCP wins when ordered reliable delivery matters (HTTP, DBs, payment APIs, file download); UDP wins when low overhead and loss tolerance matter (DNS queries, VoIP, gaming) and underpins QUIC for HTTP/3.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one TCP connection but still hits TCP head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3/QUIC over UDP isolates loss per stream and adds 0-RTT benefits.

tradeoffs.topic: Short polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Short polling is simple but wasteful; long polling reduces empty responses but stays HTTP-heavy; SSE fits server→client feeds/dashboards/notifications with EventSource reconnect; WebSockets fit chat/multiplayer/collab where both sides push often, at the cost of fan-out, reconnect, and sticky routing.
Network failure, latency, and partial failure make remote calls unlike local calls; REST/HTTP wins public APIs and tooling; RPC such as gRPC is common inside the datacenter.

tradeoffs.topic: High DNS TTL vs low DNS TTL
tradeoffs.strong_answer: High TTL speeds cache hits but leaves stale IPs after failover/deploy; low TTL improves freshness at the cost of more resolver load and slightly higher p99 latency.

tradeoffs.topic: TLS termination at edge/LB vs at the app
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Edge/LB termination offloads CPU but moves the trust boundary; mTLS for service-to-service is a separate concern from edge HTTPS termination.

tradeoffs.topic: Domain sharding on HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Sharding helped HTTP/1.1 bypass per-host connection limits and HOL pain, but can hurt HTTP/2 which benefits from multiplexing on fewer connections.

gotchas.trap: Always choosing WebSockets for any real-time feature
gotchas.correction: WebSockets bring connection state, reconnect storms, proxy/LB sticky affinity, and horizontal scaling pain; SSE or long-poll is often enough for server→client push.

gotchas.trap: Assuming HTTP/2 multiplexing removes head-of-line blocking entirely
gotchas.correction: App-layer multiplexing still suffers TCP head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3/QUIC isolates loss per stream.

gotchas.trap: Treating millions of open sockets as a non-issue on ordinary app servers
gotchas.correction: Use dedicated connection servers, pub/sub fan-out, heartbeats, timeouts, and regional gateways; account for RAM and file-descriptor cost per connection.

gotchas.trap: Setting DNS TTL without considering failover vs resolver load
gotchas.correction: TTL too high → stale IPs after failover/deploy; TTL too low → more resolver load and slightly higher p99 latency.
Termination at edge/LB offloads CPU but moves the trust boundary; app termination keeps crypto closer to the service; mTLS for service-to-service is a separate design.
Both are HTTP-friendly, but SSE is a long-lived server→client stream with browser-native EventSource reconnect; long polling reopens a full request per event and is the legacy fallback.
